name: Hong Kong
title: Hong Kong Ship UTM and Thickness Measurement Services
description: Thickness measurement in Hong Kong for HK-flag and managed ships: hull structure UTM at Kwai Tsing, anchorages and Tsing Yi yards, plus CAP gauging.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement and Ship Inspection in Hong Kong
intro: Hong Kong is one of the world's great ship-management, ship-finance and ship-registry centres, with its own maritime administration and one of the largest flag registers. Many technical decisions for ships trading worldwide are made here, while ships call at Kwai Tsing, work cargo at mid-stream buoys and anchorages, or come to the Tsing Yi repair yards. Atlantis technicians travel from India to the ship, whether it lies in Hong Kong waters or in a yard elsewhere in Asia where its Hong Kong managers need the gauging done.

highlights.p: Ships at the designated anchorages for bunkers, stores, crew change or orders are out of cargo operations. In ballast, holds and tanks can be opened, which makes an anchorage stop a practical window for pre-purchase and pre-survey readings.

highlights.h: One method across a managed fleet
highlights.p: Hong Kong managers run ships that dock all over Asia. Keeping the same measurement approach and report layout from one ship and one yard to the next makes condition records comparable across the fleet.

highlights.h: Flag and port state in one office
highlights.p: The Marine Department runs the Hong Kong register, inspects Hong Kong-flag ships and carries out port state control. Gauging suspect structure and piping beforehand lets managers fix defects on their own schedule.

port.h: Hong Kong: registry, management centre and working port
p: Hong Kong's maritime weight lies as much in its offices as in its harbour. The Hong Kong Shipping Register, run by the Marine Department, is one of the largest flag registers in the world, and the city is home to ship managers, owners, banks and lessors, P&I and hull insurers, brokers and maritime arbitrators serving fleets across Asia and beyond. A technical superintendent in Hong Kong may be responsible for ships trading anywhere, and many sale-and-purchase, chartering and survey decisions are taken here before a ship ever comes near the harbour.

The harbour itself is still a working port. The Kwai Tsing container terminals handle mainline and regional container services; mid-stream operations, where cargo is worked between ships and barges at buoys and anchorages, continue alongside terminal handling; and the designated anchorages hold ships bunkering, changing crew, taking stores or waiting for orders. River trade vessels and barges link Hong Kong with ports up the Pearl River, and with ferries crossing constantly the harbour is crowded with small craft, so launch transfers are timed by the agent around traffic as well as weather. Ship repair yards on Tsing Yi carry out afloat repairs on tankers, gas carriers, container ships and bulk carriers, and ships needing a drydock often go to yards across the boundary in Shenzhen or elsewhere in the Delta.

For inspection, that mix gives Hong Kong two roles. Ships at the anchorages or at Kwai Tsing can be gauged directly — pre-purchase inspections for buyers, on-hire and off-hire condition records, and targeted checks of tanks and piping before a survey. And Hong Kong-based managers and owners commission gauging for their ships in Chinese, Southeast Asian and other yards, where continuity of method and report format between one docking and the next matters as much as the readings themselves. Our team can be mobilised to Hong Kong waters or to wherever the ship docks.

facilities.h: Anchorages, terminals and yards in Hong Kong waters
p: Anchorage work is central in Hong Kong. A ship at one of the designated anchorages for bunkers, crew change or orders is out of cargo operations and, in ballast, can open holds and tanks; the agent books the launch that takes the team out. At Kwai Tsing, container ships allow deck, coaming, piping and scrubber work within their berth time, and ships at the Tsing Yi repair yards can be gauged during afloat repairs, with access to tanks and machinery spaces as the repair programme allows.

The Marine Department, as both flag and port authority, is also part of the picture. Hong Kong-registered ships are subject to flag state inspection, and ships calling at Hong Kong are subject to port state control, so a superintendent preparing a ship for either may want structure, tanks and piping gauged in advance. Ships working cargo at the mid-stream buoys are a different case again: they are busy with barges on both sides, and gauging there is limited to deck structure, fittings and piping that can be reached without entering the cargo working area.
list: Kwai Tsing Container Terminals — mainline and regional container ships; hatch coaming and deck plate readings and scrubber pipe checks during the terminal's working window.
Designated anchorages — ships stopping for bunkers, stores, crew or orders; holds and tanks gauged by a launch-borne team for sales, charters and survey preparation.
Mid-stream buoys — deck, fitting and piping gauging on ships working cargo to barges, scheduled around the cargo operation.
Tsing Yi ship repair yards — tank, piping and structural gauging during afloat repairs on tankers, gas carriers and bulk carriers.
Yards elsewhere in Asia for Hong Kong-managed ships — renewal survey and CAP gauging wherever the managers have booked the docking.

context.h: Hong Kong's maritime administration and market context
p: Hong Kong is a member of the Tokyo MoU in its own right, separate from mainland China, and the Marine Department carries out port state control on foreign ships as well as flag state inspection on Hong Kong-registered ships. Hong Kong also applies its own fuel rules for vessels in its waters, setting a sulphur limit for the fuel ships use there. China's domestic emission control rules take over once a ship enters mainland waters, so scrubber-fitted ships trading between the two meet different regimes within a short passage.

The market is shaped more by the managers and owners who sit in Hong Kong than by the port's own traffic. Hong Kong ship managers run tankers, bulk carriers, container ships and gas carriers for owners worldwide, and lessors and banks with Hong Kong desks hold ships as owners or as security. For them, gauging is a decision tool: a pre-purchase thickness survey before a sale, CAP gauging to keep an older tanker acceptable to charterers, an off-hire record at the end of a lease, or pre-docking data to fix a yard specification. A consistent method from one ship and one yard to the next is what makes those records comparable.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Hong Kong
jobs.p: Hong Kong jobs fall into two groups: ships gauged in Hong Kong waters, and ships managed from Hong Kong that need gauging wherever they dock. In both cases the scope is agreed with the managers' technical team, the team is mobilised from India for a confirmed window, and the report follows the layout the managers use across their fleet. The managers receive readings in the class TM formats.
list: Pre-purchase inspection in Hong Kong waters: gauging of a Hong Kong-flag bulk carrier at a designated anchorage while it bunkers, covering holds, ballast tanks and hatch covers for the buyer.
Off-hire condition gauging of a container ship at Kwai Tsing at the end of a charter, with deck, coaming and accessible tank readings recorded for both parties.
Fuel and ballast piping gauging on a tanker during afloat repairs at a Tsing Yi yard, ahead of an oil-major vetting inspection.
CAP gauging on a Hong Kong-managed Aframax docked in a mainland Chinese yard, with the managers' superintendent setting the scope from Hong Kong.
Ballast tanks and deck piping on a gas carrier measured at anchorage in Hong Kong waters, giving the Delta yard it is bound for a steel and pipe estimate in advance.

logistics: The team lands at Hong Kong International Airport. The agent books launches to the anchorages around the ship's position and the weather; Kwai Tsing and the Tsing Yi yards need terminal or yard passes arranged by the agent or the yard. Hong Kong has its own entry rules for Indian passport holders, separate from the mainland, and we confirm what is needed for each assignment before travel. For ships docking across the boundary in Shenzhen or Guangdong, the team also needs a Chinese visa, which takes longer to arrange.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a ship at a Hong Kong anchorage while it bunkers or changes crew?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A ship at anchorage for bunkers, stores or crew change is not working cargo, and if it is in ballast its holds and some tanks can be opened. We plan the scope with the superintendent around the expected stay, board by launch, and concentrate on the spaces that matter for the purpose — a sale, a charter or the next survey. The master's bunkering procedures decide which spaces and deck areas can be entered while fuel is being transferred.

faqs.q: We manage the ship from Hong Kong but it docks in mainland China — can you cover that?
faqs.a: Yes. Mobilising to a mainland yard is part of the same planning; the differences are the Chinese visa and the yard's own access arrangements. Keeping the same measurement approach and report format across the ships you manage, whichever yard they dock in, makes the records easier to compare from one survey to the next.

faqs.q: How do tropical cyclone signals affect a Hong Kong job?
faqs.a: When a tropical cyclone warning signal is raised and conditions worsen, launch services and harbour operations stop and ships may shift anchorage. Anchorage gauging pauses until services resume, while work inside a yard or on a ship at a sheltered berth may continue at the master's or yard's discretion. In the typhoon season we keep spare days in the plan for that reason.

faqs.q: Is a Hong Kong flag state inspection a reason to gauge in advance?
faqs.a: It can be. The Marine Department inspects Hong Kong-registered ships, and like port state control officers its inspectors look at structural condition, corrosion and the state of safety-critical piping. Gauging suspect deck areas, air pipes, ventilators and the fire main before an expected inspection lets the managers repair defects on their own schedule rather than under a deficiency.
